# Teratogenesis

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Pediatrics > Neonatology > Teratogenesis*

[Original Article Link](/library/V40GRT)

---

## Summary

Teratogenesis plays an important role in neonatology and is a common cause of <u>intellectual disability</u>. <u>Teratogens</u> are environmental factors that result in permanent structural or functional <u>malformations</u> or <u>death</u> of the embryo or fetus. Many congenital <u>malformations</u> are of unknown origin, but known <u>teratogens</u> include drugs, maternal illnesses and infections, <u>metal toxicity</u>, and physical agents (e.g., radiation). The fetus is most susceptible in the 3<sup>rd</sup>–8<sup>th</sup> weeks of <u>pregnancy</u> during <u>organogenesis</u> in the <u>embryonic period</u>; after 8 weeks, growth and function are affected. The earlier the exposure to the <u>teratogenic agent</u> in utero, the more severe the defects are in the embryo/fetus. However, the individual response to <u>teratogens</u> is highly varied and depends on genetic susceptibility and severity of the exposure.




See “<u>Pharmacotherapy during pregnancy</u>” for more information on <u>teratogenic drugs</u> during <u>pregnancy</u>.




See “<u>Congenital TORCH infections</u>” for more information on <u>teratogenic</u> infectious agents.

---

## Overview

* Teratogen: an environmental factor that causes a permanent structural or functional abnormality, growth restriction, or <u>death</u> of the embryo or fetus

* Effects depend on multiple factors

* The pharmacological properties, dose, and regimen of drug exposure determine the risk of developing <u>teratogenic</u> <u>birth</u> defects.

* Stage of <u>pregnancy</u> in which exposure occurs





| Overview of mechanisms of teratogenesis |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Phase | Stage in <u>pregnancy</u> | Significance |
| Preimplantation phase | <br>* 0–15 days after <u>fertilization</u>: early <u>embryonic period</u><br><br> | <br>* Toxicity to the developing embryo can cause <u>spontaneous abortion</u> (all-or-nothing effect).<br><br> |
| Embryonic phase | <br>* <u>First trimester</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Corresponds to the period of <u>organogenesis</u><br><br>* Most significant period for <u>teratogenic</u> <u>birth</u> defects<br><br><br> |
| Phase of fetal growth and maturation | <br>* Second and third trimesters<br><br> | <br><br>* Period of fetal growth and maturation<br><br>* Can lead to deficits in organ function, intellect, behavior, or minor structural <u>malformations</u><br><br><br> |




* The physical effects of <u>teratogens</u> are widely varied (see individual conditions for specific manifestations).

* VACTERL association [[1]](/library/6YYjJn)

* Vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal <u>fistula</u>, renal, and limb abnormalities

* Due to a defect during the development of embryonic <u>mesoderm</u>

* Limb deformities

* Syndactyly: fusion of two or more fingers or toes (most common congenital <u>malformation</u> of the limbs)

* Polymelia/polydactyly: supernumerary limbs, fingers, or toes

* Oligodactyly, adactyly: absence of one or more of the fingers or toes

* Ectromelia: collective term for <u>hypoplasia</u> and/or <u>aplasia</u> of one or more <u>long bones</u>, resulting in limb deformity

* Peromelia/perodactyly: <u>amputation</u>-like stump of a limb, finger, or toe

## Maternal conditions

### <u>Diabetes mellitus</u> (<u>pregestational diabetes mellitus</u> or <u>gestational diabetes mellitus</u>) [[2]](/library/JYYsJn)




* <u>Diabetic embryopathy</u>

* <u>Diabetic fetopathy</u>

* For more information, see “<u>Fetal and neonatal complications of diabetes mellitus in pregnancy</u>” in "<u>Diabetes mellitus in pregnancy</u>."





### <u>Obesity</u> [[3]](/library/xw1EOQ0)




* <u>Preterm birth</u>

* <u>Stillbirth</u>

* <u>Neural tube defects</u>

* <u>Congenital heart disease</u>

* <u>Cleft lip</u>, <u>cleft palate</u>

* Limb reduction abnormalities

* <u>Macrosomia</u>





### <u>Graves disease</u> [[4]](/library/kE1mDi0)




* <u>Neonatal hyperthyroidism</u>

* <u>Preterm birth</u>

* <u>Stillbirth</u>

* <u>Intrauterine growth restriction</u>

* <u>Low birth weight</u>

* Developmental and behavioral problems





### <u>Hypothyroidism</u>




* <u>Congenital hypothyroidism</u>

* <u>Congenital iodine deficiency syndrome</u>





### <u>Phenylketonuria</u> (<u>maternal PKU</u>) [[5]](/library/Cqaq0N)[[6]](/library/OE1IDi0)



* Phenylalanine embryopathy

* Definition: the developmental <u>malformations</u> in a <u>newborn</u> resulting from <u>PKU</u> during <u>pregnancy</u>

* Clinical findings

* <u>Intrauterine growth restriction</u>

* <u>Microcephaly</u>

* <u>Congenital heart disease</u>

* <u>Intellectual disability</u>

* Developmental problems

## Risks of substance use during pregnancy

For information on screening and management of <u>substance use during pregnancy</u>, see “<u>Prenatal psychosocial screening</u>.”




### <u>Alcohol</u>: fetal alcohol syndrome (embryo-fetal <u>alcohol</u> syndrome) [[7]](/library/zqaraN)




#### <u>Epidemiology</u>




* Most common cause of <u>teratogenic</u> damage in children (0.2–1.5 per 1,000 <u>live births</u>) [[8]](/library/Q-buCw)

* Most common preventable cause of <u>intellectual disability</u> in the US





#### Mechanism of teratogenesis



* Failed neuronal and <u>glial cell</u> migration




#### Clinical findings




* Dysmorphic features ;  [[9]](/library/IYYYqn)

* Thin upper lip

* Smooth <u>hypoplastic</u> <u>philtrum</u>

* Down-slanting, short <u>palpebral fissures</u>

* <u>Hypertelorism</u>

* <u>Microcephaly</u>

* <u>Epicanthal folds</u>

* Receding chin

* Features of specific systemic defects

* <u>Heart</u> defects (mainly <u>ventricular septal defect</u>)

* <u>Heart</u>-<u>lung</u> <u>fistulas</u>

* Skeletal anomalies (limb <u>dislocations</u>, <u>joint contractures</u>, <u>pectus excavatum</u>/<u>pectus carinatum</u>)

* Holoprosencephaly: a developmental <u>field defect</u> in which the forebrain fails to divide into two hemispheres, resulting in fusion of ventricles (leading to the formation of monoventricle) and other bilateral cerebral structures, e.g., <u>basal ganglia</u>  ;  [[10]](/library/qYYCJn)

* Most commonly occurs during the 3<sup>rd</sup>–4<sup>th</sup> week of <u>pregnancy</u> [[11]](/library/bEXH8-)

* Potential genetic causes include:

* Mutations in <u>SHH gene</u> coding for <u>sonic hedgehog</u> protein

* <u>Trisomy 13</u>

* Associated clinical features

* Craniofacial abnormalities (<u>cyclopia</u>, <u>cleft lip</u>/<u>palate</u>, <u>hypotelorism</u>, and/or proboscis)

* Endocrine disorders related to <u>pituitary</u> dysfunction (e.g., <u>diabetes insipidus</u>)

* <u>Seizures and epilepsy</u>

* Renal anomalies (aplastic/<u>dysplastic</u> <u>kidneys</u>) leading to <u>hypertension</u>

* Prenatal or postnatal growth retardation → <u>short stature</u>

* Other

* Hyperactivity

* <u>Intellectual disability</u> (e.g., impaired <u>language development</u>, <u>learning</u> disabilities, <u>memory</u> deficits), and subsequent problems in social interactions and school performance

* Differential diagnoses

* <u>Down syndrome</u>

* <u>Fragile-X syndrome</u>

* <u>Williams syndrome</u>

### Risk of tobacco product use during pregnancy [[12]](/library/rYYfqn)[[13]](/library/7YY4qn)




* Mechanism of teratogenesis

* <u>Nicotine</u>: ↑ <u>catecholamine</u> release → <u>vasoconstriction</u> of uteroplacental blood vessels → compromised blood flow and <u>oxygen delivery</u> to the fetus

* <u>Carbon monoxide</u>: ↑ <u>COHb</u> causes tissue <u>hypoxia</u>

* Effects

* <u>Intrauterine growth restriction</u>

* <u>Low birth weight</u>

* Increased risk of <u>preterm labor</u> and <u>miscarriage</u> (e.g., due to <u>placental</u> abnormalities such as <u>placental abruption</u>)

* <u>Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder</u> (<u>ADHD</u>) and <u>conduct disorder</u>

* <u>Sudden infant death syndrome</u> (<u>SIDS</u>)

* <u>Cleft lip</u> and <u>palate</u>

* See “<u>Tobacco product use in pregnancy and postpartum</u>” for information on screening and management.





### <u>Opioids</u>




* Mechanism of teratogenesis [[14]](/library/pE1L9i0)

* Not entirely understood.

* Altered levels of <u>neurotransmitters</u> (<u>norepinephrine</u>, <u>dopamine</u>, and <u>serotonin</u>) are believed to play a role.

* Effects

* Respiratory <u>depression</u>

* <u>Neonatal abstinence syndrome</u>

* <u>Intrauterine growth restriction</u>

* <u>Low birth weight</u>

* Fetal dysgenesis

* <u>Placental abruption</u>





### <u>Cocaine</u> [[15]](/library/sYYtqn)




* Mechanism of teratogenesis: <u>cocaine</u> → <u>vasoconstriction</u> of the uteroplacental <u>placental</u> vessels→ compromised blood flow and <u>oxygen delivery</u> to the fetus

* Effects

* <u>Intrauterine growth retardation</u>

* <u>Low birth weight</u>

* <u>Preterm labor</u>

* <u>Placental abruption</u>

## Medications

The following drugs are no longer approved for clinical use. See “<u>Pharmacotherapy during pregnancy</u>“ for a comprehensive list of <u>teratogenic drugs</u>.




### <u>Diethylstilbestrol</u> [[16]](/library/CYYqrn)




* Previous use: a synthetic <u>estrogen</u> that is primarily used to prevent <u>miscarriages</u> in expectant mothers

* Effects

* Vaginal <u>clear cell</u> <u>adenocarcinoma</u>

* Congenital anomalies of the <u>Müllerian duct</u>





### Thalidomide [[17]](/library/xYYErn)




* Previous use: a sedative that is used to treat <u>nausea</u> or <u>vomiting</u> in pregnant women (now administered in limited indications, e.g., <u>multiple myeloma</u>)

* Effects: thalidomide embryopathy

* Symmetrical amelia (complete absence of limbs)

* <u>Micromelia</u> (“flipper limbs”)

* <u>Anotia</u> (absence of the external <u>ear</u>)

* Phocomelia: a <u>teratogenic</u> limb defect that is characterized by the absence of the <u>proximal</u> portion of a limb (hand or foot are directly attached to the shoulder or hip)





> [!NOTE]
> ThaLIMBdomide causes LIMB defects.

## Metal toxicity

### Lead [[19]](/library/zYYr7n)




* Etiology: maternal <u>lead poisoning</u> (blood Pb â¥ 50 Î¼g/dL)

* Effects

* <u>Spontaneous abortion</u>

* <u>Stillbirth</u>

* <u>Hemangiomas</u>, <u>lymphangiomas</u>, <u>hydroceles</u>, <u>skin tags</u>, <u>undescended testes</u>

* <u>VACTERL</u> [[20]](/library/_YY57n)





### <u>Mercury</u> [[21]](/library/ZbYZHn)




* Etiology: methylmercury (can be found in contaminated seafood, esp. tilefish, swordfish, shark, and king mackerel)

* Effects

* <u>Cerebellar</u> <u>atrophy</u>

* <u>Atrophy</u> of the visual <u>brain cortex</u>

* Polyneuritis
